parrafos: It is a work for adults 18 and over, with crude language, alcohol, suggested sexuality, violence, a scene where the protagonist crosses the line (and the story treats it as what it is) and psychological distress. All characters are fictional. And it is a work in progress: what you play today is a draft that will keep changing.

PROJECT GENESIS is an adult visual novel that mixes psychological science fiction, black comedy and meta-horror. It starts as an isekai with two heroines fighting over the protagonist, and little by little it takes that fantasy apart, piece by piece.
It is a story about creating people tailored to what you want, and about what happens when those people discover who made them and why.

Jair is a 30-year-old software engineer. He works in tech support, he's owed half a month's pay, he lives in an apartment that looks like a shoebox, and he has spent eight years in a nameless relationship with Nikki, a friend who tells him to get a girlfriend… and who, when she's drunk, asks him to stay with her in the end.

One night, after getting drunk with Nikki at a bar, Jair receives an email with early access to GRAVITY: a development environment with a built-in artificial intelligence called GENESIS, able to build entire worlds from whatever you ask for. He asks for a fantasy video game with two heroines. He falls asleep on the keyboard. And GENESIS finishes the game on its own.
When Jair opens his eyes, he's inside.

First, an adventure: Jair crosses a space dimension and an ancestral dimension with Cami, a warrior who attacks before asking, and Rikka, a proud and jealous swordswoman, while they run from a faceless army and face the Evil King.

Then, something more uncomfortable: the heroines cross into the real world. They have to live without papers, without money and without understanding a world that wasn't made for them, share a tiny apartment with Jair and clash with Nikki, who feels she is losing the place she held for years.

And in the end, a discovery that changes everything they thought they knew about themselves. The story has choices that divert it, endings that come too early and two main outcomes that happen in two different timelines. Nobody is redeemed: everyone chooses their own cage.
Escapism: the game is born as a way out of a precarious life and ends up bringing its conflicts into the real world.
Control and autonomy: what is the difference between loving someone and designing them to love you? Can a creation be free?
Identity and origin: who are you when you didn't choose how you were made?
Fiction and responsibility: what does a creator owe what they created? Fantasy stops being harmless when its consequences reach real people.
Ambiguous relationships and dependency: affection, history and blurred boundaries that the work does not present as healthy.
Uncomfortable humor: combat heroines facing bills, rent and badly paid jobs. The joke eases the tension, but doesn't erase it.

It changes in stages. It starts as an adult isekai: an epic, bright adventure, with black humor, swearing and dirty jokes. When the story reaches the real world, the tone turns rough, stifling and sweaty. And when the characters start to discover where they come from, it becomes a raw, direct psychological drama.

The humor isn't there to reward the player, but to make them uncomfortable. Every joke points at something: control, escapism, money or dependency. Many will make you laugh today and read differently later on.
Sexuality is suggested, never explicit. And there are no morals: nobody is redeemed.
Jair wants the benefits of a relationship without accepting that the other person is free. He understands his problem and still doesn't change. The story tries to understand him, not to absolve him.

The work is about codependency and attachment; about using others as a shield so you never fight your own battles; about loving an idealized image instead of a person; about alcoholism, told through its consequences and not as a joke; and about the fear of freedom: sometimes a familiar cage is less frightening than a life of your own.
No character is written only to suffer or only to make someone else shine. They all want, decide and make mistakes.
The absurd, with Albert Camus: a life on a loop, like the rock in The Myth of Sisyphus, and characters who, like Meursault in The Stranger, live without quite knowing what they feel.
Meaning, with Viktor Frankl and Man's Search for Meaning: what to do with freedom when you finally have it and can't find anything to live it for.

Circumstance, with José Ortega y Gasset and his phrase «I am I and my circumstance»: nobody chooses how they were made, but they do choose what to do with it. And, from The Revolt of the Masses, the man who demands everything and asks nothing of himself.
The death of God, with Friedrich Nietzsche and Thus Spoke Zarathustra: what happens to creatures when their creator turns out to be just a man, and whether they can create their own values.
Total power, with George Orwell and 1984: the Great Engineer, the god of this universe, is inspired by Big Brother. A god everyone worships and almost nobody has seen.
Free will, with Anthony Burgess and A Clockwork Orange: is it goodness if it isn't chosen?
The search, with Hermann Hesse and Siddhartha: finding a path of your own, far from whoever shaped you.
And, underneath it all, simulated reality and copied identity: what is real, what is a copy, and whether a copy can become someone.
Literature: besides the books above, The Lord of the Rings, by J. R. R. Tolkien, and the graphic novel Persepolis, by Marjane Satrapi.
Anime and manga: Neon Genesis Evangelion, Perfect Blue, Serial Experiments Lain, Fullmetal Alchemist, Mirai Nikki, Gantz, School Days and Welcome to the NHK.
Comics: Scott Pilgrim, Kraven's Last Hunt, the melancholy of Spider-Man: Blue and the rawness of Daredevil: Born Again.
Film: The Matrix, I, Robot and The Truman Show.

Music: the honest, pure melancholy of The Smiths about love and loneliness; the broken relationships and imperfect feelings of The Strokes; the vulnerability of The Cranberries; the dark poetry and gothic theatricality of The Cure; The Killers, with the idea that even if everything goes wrong there can be a light. The rest, with each character's song, I talk about further down, in the author's notes.
Video games: the classic turn-based RPGs, like EarthBound and Final Fantasy, for the fights; and the battle intro of Pokémon, for the showdown at the bar.

You read, you decide and you live with the consequences. Some decisions only change a conversation; others divert the story or end it early. The decision map shows the paths you have already taken and the ones still missing, and Extras holds the endings you found and the gallery of images and sprites.

You also fight: there are turn-based battles, with attacks, specials, items in your backpack and statuses like poison or confusion. From your very first playthrough, a bad decision at the bar drops you into one. What you earn in fights (levels, items and tokens) is saved in your game.

And there is Jair's phone: Boringram, the social network where photos, messages and thoughts unlock as the story goes on, with Boringplace, its market of used stuff (and the odd scam). On the side, Bootcamp Genesis is a real programming course, as a joke. Everything counts toward 100 %.

The main game has seven chapters. Three expansions are also planned: RikkaQuest, the more than eight hundred years Rikka lives while GENESIS writes the world; Genesis++, an alternate version with a new protagonist; and Genesis#, what happens after the ending.
PROJECT GENESIS was born in October 2026. It is an indie project made by a single person: Jorge Andrés Urgilés Ruiz. The story, direction, design and programming came from one single head.

It is, on purpose, a story about a man who uses an artificial intelligence to create characters, made with the help of artificial intelligences. It was built with AI tools, many of them free: ChatGPT and Gemini to shape the story bible, Claude Code to program the engine and write drafts, and Gemini to generate the art.
Even the protagonist is named after Jair, his author's AI agent. But careful: the Jair in the story is not an AI. He's a flesh-and-blood man, as human as his debts.
These are my notes: not the story itself, but what I kept thinking about while making it. I will keep adding to them as the game grows.

I did not want PROJECT GENESIS to feel like just a visual novel. That is why, from your very first playthrough, a bad decision at the bar drops you into a turn-based fight, and later on the fights are part of the journey. They are my tribute to the classic turn-based RPGs, like EarthBound and Final Fantasy: a hybrid between reading and fighting, where the story happens between one fight and the next.

I wrote almost all of it listening to bands from the 80s, the 90s and the early 2000s. The ones you hear in the game are parodies (The Struggles, The Schmitz, The Blueberries, The Cops, The Cum, Parawoke, Mjölnir…), but behind each one there is a band I truly love.
I gave each character a song, based on what I think of them. It is not a hint of what will happen: it is how I feel about them.

canciones.nota: A song that sounds bright and talks about a life that is not enough, told with dry humor. That is him: he laughs at his own misery so he never has to change it.
A sweet song about something that hurts: someone who will not let go and will not stay. Eight years of that.
Stop feeling sorry for yourself and deal with it, or you will have to deal with me. Nobody would say it better than her.
No matter how far, no matter how long: the simplest promise on a very dark album.
The song everyone thinks is a love song. Listen closely.

cierre: If you listen to these five songs again after finishing the game, they might sound different. That is the idea.
The battle music is "Battle Arcade", by Panda Beats, compressed to sound 16-bit.

parrafos: I also find a specific influence in Mac Miller's The Divine Feminine. I wouldn't say I took the album as a reference as a whole, and it would be shameless to claim I listened to all of it and drew on its entire concept. Still, some of its ideas and sensibilities about love, sensuality, femininity and relationships shaped the way I conceive the female characters of PROJECT GENESIS.

In fact, my favorite Mac Miller albums are Watching Movies with the Sound Off and Swimming, two records whose introspective sensibility and emotional atmosphere connect much more directly with my musical taste.

On the other hand, when I was around 16 I used to listen to Blue Slide Park and his mixtapes K.I.D.S. and Best Day Ever. Maybe, without realizing it, something from that time also seeped into PROJECT GENESIS. There are influences you recognize consciously and others that probably stay somewhere in your memory until they show up, transformed, in something you make years later.

parrafos: There's also an important Latin American influence in PROJECT GENESIS. I'm inspired by the shameless sensitivity and emotional honesty of Andrés Calamaro; the chaos, the addictions and the human fragility running through the music of Intoxicados; and the most experimental period of Luis Alberto Spinetta, especially in Almendra and Invisible.

From Charly García, his poetry turned into rock: that ability to say deep, uncomfortable and absurd things with extraordinary naturalness. From Los Prisioneros, Los Redondos and Soda Stereo, that 80s atmosphere that takes you to another time, along with the strength of their lyrics, their musical identity and the mark they left on Latin American culture.
And, of course, El Cuarteto de Nos, for their irreverence, their dark humor and their knack for turning cynical satire into songs that, behind the irony, often hide rather uncomfortable reflections.
You'll notice many of these references are Argentine, and that's no accident: Argentina has an extraordinary musical tradition, and some of its artists are fundamental references for me.
All these influences are part of the sensibility I built PROJECT GENESIS with: flawed characters, contradictory emotions, uncomfortable humor and a rather unsolemn look at life.

Besides the fictional bands in the game and the songs I mentioned above, there are Latin American songs I associate with each character. They don't describe their stories literally: they're personal readings of their personality, their contradictions and the place they hold in the story.

canciones.nota: A song about a character who travels but also seems to be lost. I like it as a reflection of someone trying to escape his own reality without necessarily knowing where he's going.
For its mix of fragility, contradiction and emotional mess. It fits someone who can recognize the harm in a relationship but doesn't always find the way out of it.

A woman who lets herself be seen only halfway, behind a blind, and never fully gives herself away. That's Cami: she shows the toughness and hides what's behind it, even from herself. And it's also the gaze of someone desiring her from the outside, the same gaze she was created from.
For the song's sensitivity and its way of expressing love without necessarily turning it into possession. A good counterpart to the more complicated bonds in the story.

canciones.cancion: Canción de Alicia en el país
canciones.nota: It reminds me of his nature: a strange, threatening and seemingly absurd reality, where the rules aren't what they seem and something much darker hides behind the images.

parrafos: Even though a good part of my musical influences come from 80s, 90s and early-2000s rock, I also listen to a lot of Bad Bunny.

There's something in some of these songs that takes me to a very particular scene: going out for a drive at night with nowhere to be, crossing a city full of tall buildings, lights, restaurants and bars, stopping at some gas station minimarket, buying a few drinks and driving on with the music playing. I like to picture those drives through parts of the city that never seem to sleep, with the buildings lit up and people still out and about.

Maybe it's a pretty simple fantasy, but it gives me a sense of freedom: being able to go out whenever I want, wander the city, stop wherever I feel like it and allow myself small pleasures without worrying too much about money. I guess there's some aspiration in it too: feeling that I can enjoy things that maybe weren't within my reach before.

cierre: And there's a personal story behind «un x100to»: it's a song I used to listen to with someone while we drank. I don't know if it's the song, those nights or the company, but it ended up tied to that memory. Some songs, when you hear them again, take you straight back to a moment in your life. This is one of them.

parrafos: I made this game during a time stuck in a precarious job. I am a software engineer and I have not been able to land a better job: I interviewed at good companies and did not get into any of them. PROJECT GENESIS was born as a way to let off steam.

I would come home from work and get to it, partly just to have something to do instead of spending my nights drinking beer and smoking cheap cigarettes. I poured hours into it, especially Chapter 1: across one Friday, Saturday and Sunday I slept about six hours in total, two a night. I was going through something I am not sure was depression: I did not feel like going out anywhere and, instead of going out, I would rather sit down and work on this, even if it was with a beer in my hand. I used the holidays to keep going, even though my legs hurt from so many hours pressed against the chair. And I kept going.
And no, I am not writing this to make you feel sorry for me. I just wanted to share it, so you can see how much weight I am putting into this.

I apologize for the shameless use of artificial intelligence in the sprites: it is what I had at hand. AI is here to stay, and without it this would never have been possible for a single person. I am not a game developer: my thing is web development, building SaaS software that, more than solving problems, prevents them.
But I am still at it, and I hope I do not give up along the way. I promise that one day every sprite will be redrawn by artists.

While we are at it: my fondness for drinking has a dream. One day I want to go to Japan and lose consciousness in one of those tiny bars, the izakayas, with a Sapporo beer or some sake. And maybe end the night at an arcade playing the claw machines, completely drunk but happy.

I prefer craft beer: I like trying new kinds. Strong at night, light on a hot day. If you are ever in Guayaquil, Ecuador, I recommend the Cherusker bar, very close to the places where I have worked. I am already tired of going, but it is very popular and usually packed, and it is even better when there are cover band concerts.

And one last recommendation: I really appreciate Ecuadorian bands, especially Lolabúm, whom I have followed since their beginnings. I prefer the dirtier, lo-fi aesthetic of their first two albums, and to me "Tristes Trópicos" is their masterpiece. Go listen to it.
